title: Bosnian Police Intercept 96 Migrants, Identify Two Suspected Smugglers
content:
Bosnia and Herzegovina's border police prevented 96 people from illegally crossing the country's border, the agency said in a statement Thursday.

The smuggling attempts were thwarted in two separate operations Wednesday in the town of Bistrica. During the afternoon, officers intercepted 63 people—40 from Pakistan and 23 from Bangladesh. Acting on orders from the state prosecutor’s office, investigators seized two boats and identified two suspected smugglers.

Later that evening, authorities intercepted another 33 people in the same town, including 18 from Afghanistan, 13 from Bangladesh and two from Pakistan. Police said the country's Service for Foreigners' Affairs was notified and the investigation remains ongoing.

title: Businessman Acquitted of Commissioning Murder of Maltese Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia
content:
Nine years after investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb outside her home in Malta, businessman Yorgen Fenech has been found not guilty of complicity for allegedly masterminding her assassination.

The nine-member jury returned its verdict on the evening of September 2 after about 8 hours of deliberation, voting 8-1 on the charge of complicity and 8-1 on the other charge he faced for alleged criminal association. 

The verdict at the Law Courts in Valletta, Malta's capital, closes what has been one of the longest jury trials in the country’s history, running to 55 sitting days since it opened on July 1.

Fenech, 44, the former chief executive of the Tumas Group, had pleaded not guilty. 

The prosecution, led by Anthony Vella and Godwin Cini, is expected to appeal the verdict. It argued that Fenech commissioned and financed the killing, paying self-confessed middleman Melvin Theuma 150,000 euros ($ 170,00) to engage the hitmen, and that he passed Theuma information about the police investigation in the two years that followed. Theuma was granted a presidential pardon to testify in the case.

title: Ukraine Presidential Chief Responds to Alleged Laundering Role
content:
The head of Ukraine’s presidential office, has said courts should determine the significance of recordings that have raised questions about his involvement in an alleged $3.3 million money-laundering scheme aimed at securing bail for a former minister detained in a sprawling energy sector corruption probe.

Authorities have not publicly named Kyrylo Budanov and he has not been charged but  court documents obtained by the Ukrainian news outlet hromadske appear to identify him participating in a conversation concerning the money laundering.

Responding to questions about the tapes, Budanov told hromadske that any determination regarding the recordings should be made by a judge. “Let the court figure out who appears where,” he said.

title: Dutch Police Arrest 34 Following Drug-related Shootout
content:
Dutch authorities arrested 34 people Wednesday at various locations across the country following a deadly shootout in a Dutch village, reportedly linked to a notorious drug lord, public broadcaster NOS reported.

The incident unfolded around 4:00 a.m. Tuesday when dozens of masked men, several armed with heavy firearms, disembarked from two vans in Overasselt, near the German border. The group approached a farm belonging to a family allegedly involved in drug trafficking and opened fire on a car. The 51-year-old man inside the vehicle was killed, police told a press conference. The masked men also fired at two police officers, leaving one with life-threatening injuries.

title: Ukraine Busts Crypto Fraud Network Targeting EU Victims
content:
Ukraine’s Security Service and National Police dismantled a Kyiv-based crypto fraud network that allegedly targeted EU citizens and generated monthly turnover of up to $1 million at its peak. Investigators say the group, involving several dozen people and led by a 25-year-old IT specialist, posed as representatives of cryptocurrency platforms and lured victims with supposedly profitable investment opportunities promoted through Telegram channels.

After showing victims fictitious trading results, the suspects allegedly directed them to fake websites designed to mimic legitimate crypto services. The sites contained malicious “drainer” code that enabled unauthorized withdrawals once users connected their wallets and approved transactions. Police searched 23 offices and homes, seizing phones, computer equipment, cash believed to be criminal proceeds and 16 luxury cars, including Porsche, BMW and Mercedes-Benz vehicles. Authorities have not yet named any suspects, and the investigation is ongoing.

title: Spain Arrests Germany’s Most Wanted Drug Trafficker
content:
Spanish police, working with German authorities, have arrested Germany’s most wanted drug trafficker in the southern city of Málaga, the National Police announced Monday. The unnamed fugitive, detained on August 24, was wanted under a European arrest warrant for drug trafficking and organized crime, as well as a separate Spanish judicial warrant.

According to investigators, the suspect led a criminal network that used a warehouse in Spain to load large quantities of narcotics onto trucks bound for Germany via France. The fugitive, described as an expert in boxing and mixed martial arts, became the target of an intensive investigation in 2025 when authorities learned he was hiding in Spain.

To evade capture, the trafficker changed his phone number every two weeks and his identity every three months, police said, noting he had even taken a cybersecurity course in Turkey to learn how to avoid digital tracking. Following extensive surveillance, officers tracked down his brother and arrested the fugitive while he was riding in the passenger seat of his brother's car.

title: Q&A: What Has Emerged From the Trial of a Businessman Charged in the Murder of a Maltese Journalist?
content:
OCCRP: Daphne Caruana Galizia is said to have coined a phrase that has been picked up by anti-corruption activists: “Malta is not a normal country." Are there any aspects of this trial that bring the phrase to mind now that the lawyers have made their final arguments, and the jury will soon reach its verdict?

Julian Bonnici: The political shadow over the case is a long one. Keith Schembri, the former chief of staff to Malta's ex-prime minister spent close to four days in the witness box, and has been accused throughout the trial of being the real mastermind. He denies it, and little hard evidence for it has been put before the jury.

The trial has also laid out defendant Yorgen Fenech's web of contacts across Malta's political elite: his WhatsApp exchanges with Schembri, with former Prime Minister Joseph Muscat, with regulatory heads, and with the deputy police commissioner who once headed the investigation into the murder.

A lot of people know that Caruana Galizia was Malta’s most prominent investigative journalist and anti-corruption activist. Who is Yorgen Fenech, and what is the prosecution alleging motivated him to commission her murder?

title: Uganda Arrests 16 in Alleged $4M Fake Gold Scam
content:
Ugandan police have arrested 16 people, including four police officers, for their alleged involvement in a fake gold scam that defrauded a Dubai businessman of $4 million, the Uganda Police Force stated.

The suspects operated under the company name Real Sunnex Ltd and allegedly obtained the $4 million from an unnamed Dubai businessman through a fake gold transaction. According to investigators, the group was also preparing to obtain another $4 million from the businessman using a similar scheme. Investigators also said the four officers had abandoned their duties to guard the suspected fraudsters at an illegal gold refinery.

The investigation followed a complaint filed by the businessman in July 2025, in which he named Asiimwe Moses as one of the alleged fraudsters and identified the company as Real Sunnex Ltd. During the operation, police recovered fake gold, documents and eight vehicles.

title: Australia Probes Western Union Over Possible Money Laundering Risks
content:
Australia’s financial intelligence agency AUSTRAC has launched an investigation into Western Union Financial Services Australia and its U.S.-based parent company over concerns about how they manage money laundering and terrorism financing risks. The probe will examine the company’s anti-money laundering program, transaction monitoring and governance, including whether its systems can identify known laundering typologies and suspicious transactions linked to child sexual exploitation and terrorism financing.

The investigation follows previous regulatory engagement and an external audit ordered in 2025. Western Union operates one of the world’s largest international money transfer networks, including cash-based cross-border payments, a sector considered particularly vulnerable to criminal exploitation. Regulators have identified risks in the sector including fraud, human trafficking, terrorism financing and child sexual exploitation. Western Union has committed to addressing issues raised in the audit.

title: South Africa Arrests Suspect in $37M Hospital Corruption Case
content:
South Africa’s Hawks arrested a 37-year-old man in an investigation into corruption, procurement fraud and money laundering involving 635 million rand ($37 million) at Tembisa Hospital. He was detained at Johannesburg’s O.R. Tambo International Airport after returning from abroad. Investigators say hospital officials colluded with service providers to keep individual transactions below 500,000 rand and bypass formal tender procedures. He is expected to face fraud, corruption and money laundering charges in a Specialized Commercial Crimes Court. Authorities have not named the man.

The arrest is part of a broader investigation into claims that more than 2 billion rand was looted from the public hospital. South Africa’s Special Investigating Unit previously identified three coordinated syndicates that it says used networks of companies and thousands of irregular transactions to divert hospital funds. The procurement activity was initially flagged by Gauteng Health Department whistleblower Babita Deokaran, who was murdered in 2021.

title: Alleged Narco-Terrorist Moves to Toss U.S. Indictment on Jurisdictional Grounds
content:
Attorneys for the accused South American drug kingpin Sebastián Marset have filed motions to dismiss all drug trafficking, money laundering, and narco-terrorism charges against him, challenging the U.S. government’s authority to prosecute the case.

Marset is seeking a complete dismissal of the indictment, alleging that agents of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) interrogated him without advising him of his Miranda rights, denied him access to counsel, and brought vindictive charges after he rejected a plea deal. His defense team has also filed motions accusing DEA agents of attempting to extort cryptocurrency from him.

However, Marset’s primary defense rests on a novel jurisdictional argument. His lawyers contend that the United States lacks the authority to prosecute him because the alleged offenses took place outside the country. Prosecutors accuse Marset of leading a massive cartel that shipped cocaine from South America to Europe, with illicit proceeds allegedly wired back to South America through banks in Hong Kong and China.

title: Slovak Police Foil Possible Napalm Attack on Factory Producing Drones for Ukraine
content:
Officers from ÚBOK—Slovakia’s Office for the Fight Against Organized Crime—thwarted a potential arson attack on the Skyeton factory near Prešov, which manufactures unmanned systems for the Ukrainian military, police announced earlier this week.

The Ukrainian company's Raybird-3 drones can stay airborne for up to 28 hours and travel up to 2,500 kilometers, operating deep behind enemy lines.

Had the attack succeeded, police said, it would have risked a large-scale fire, endangered the roughly 70 employees who could have been on site, and caused damage worth tens of millions of dollars.

The Slovak Information Service and Military Intelligence played a key role in uncovering the plot, providing information that prompted ÚBOK to launch an intensive investigation. Police identified the perpetrators before the attack could take place and seized a large quantity of incendiary mixture—identified by the Police Force's Institute of Forensic Science as a blend of gasoline and polystyrene commonly known as napalm—along with tools, a mobile phone, an action camera and a hand-drawn plan of the attack.

title: Singapore Police Probe 231 Suspected Scam Mules
content:
Singapore police are investigating 231 people suspected of acting as scammers or money mules in more than 721 fraud cases that caused about S$4.1 million (US$3.2 million) in losses, authorities said Thursday.

The 149 men and 82 women, aged between 15 and 76, were identified during a two-week operation by the Cyber Command and seven police divisions. The cases involve e-commerce, phishing, job and investment scams, as well as government official impersonation and fake lucky draws.

Police are investigating the suspects for alleged cheating, money laundering or providing payment services without a license. Cheating and money laundering offenses can each carry prison terms of up to 10 years. Some scammers and people who recruit others for scam syndicates may also face mandatory caning of between six and 24 strokes.

Money mules who help move criminal proceeds or provide SIM cards or Singpass credentials can face discretionary caning of up to 12 strokes. Police said suspected mules may also have their banking services and mobile subscriptions restricted under Singapore’s Facility Restriction Framework.

title: Malaysia’s Ex-Prime Minister Charged Over Failure to Declare Assets
content:
A Malaysian court charged former Prime Minister Ismail Sabri Yaakob on Thursday with failing to disclose his assets to the country’s anti-graft agency. According to state news agency Bernama, the 66-year-old is accused of failing to declare local and foreign currencies totaling nearly $40 million, as well as five gold bars, to the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) on February 7 last year at the agency's headquarters.

Ismail Sabri, who served as Malaysia's prime minister from August 2021 to October 2022, pleaded not guilty to the charges and was released on 300,000 ringgit (about $74,500) bail.

He submitted a wealth declaration to the MACC in March last year after the agency seized the $40 million in assets allegedly linked to him as part of a broader investigation into corruption and money laundering.

The next hearing in the trial is set for September 29.

title: OCCRP Denounces Police Search of Solomon Islands Reporter
content:
OCCRP has strongly condemned the Solomon Island police for questioning one of the network’s member center journalists and searching her office in an effort to identify her government whistleblower. 

Officers questioned the reporter and searched her office for a confidential document used in an investigation last year. The story revealed that auditors had raised concerns over a $10 billion tax discrepancy involving the Solomon Islands Tobacco Company, a subsidiary of British American Tobacco.

Gina Maka’a, an investigative reporter for In-depth Solomons, told OCCRP that she initially spoke by phone on Tuesday morning with an officer of the Royal Solomon Islands Police Force (RSIPF), who told her that she needed to hand over a document they believed was in her possession. Then the officer showed up at her workplace in the capital, Honiara. 

She was asked to hand over the original paper copy of the document used in the report. Maka’a told the officer the document was no longer in her possession. When asked to name the person who gave it to her, she refused.

She was then shown a search warrant bearing the name of another person, the former head of the local press association, Georgina Kekea.
snippet: OCCRP has strongly condemned the Solomon Island police for questioning one of the network’s member center journalists and searching her office in an effort to identify her government whistleblower.

title: ‘I Had No Involvement. Zero.’: Accused Mastermind Denies Killing Maltese Journalist
content:
The Maltese businessman accused of commissioning the 2017 car-bomb assassination of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia took the stand to adamantly deny ordering her death, even as he admitted to delivering tens of thousands of euros to the plot's middleman and passing along leaked police intelligence.

"I never ordered the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia," the defendant, Yorgen Fenech, told jurors during four days of testimony. "I had no involvement. Zero."

Fenech, 44, former chief executive of the Tumas Group and a major shareholder in a state power consortium, unexpectedly waived his right to remain silent to deliver his first public account of the crime since his 2019 arrest. He claimed Keith Schembri, the influential former chief of staff to former Prime Minister Joseph Muscat, framed him.

Schembri, who testified earlier in the trial, has denied any involvement, and police told jurors he was never considered a suspect.

title: Armenian Court Orders Son of Ex-President Held in Sweeping Graft Probe
content:
A court in Yerevan ordered the eldest son of former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan held in pretrial detention on Wednesday, expanding a sweeping corruption investigation that has ensnared the former leader and several high-ranking ex-officials.

The decision to hold Sedrak Kocharyan for two months followed his detention on Tuesday alongside his father. Investigators carried out coordinated raids on family-linked real estate and commercial holdings, escalating a long-running political battle between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and the country's former ruling elite.

Lawyers for the younger Kocharyan said they would appeal the ruling, with defense attorney Alexander Kochubayev describing the case as an "extralegal prosecution" driven by political motives.

Armenia’s Anti-Corruption Committee stated that the elder Kocharyan, who served as president from 1998 to 2008, used his office to acquire state property at artificially low prices and accept substantial bribes. Officials said several prime parcels of land were improperly funneled to the family and later developed into commercial ventures.

title: Designed for Impact: The Next Evolution of OCCRP’s Website
content:
Welcome to the new OCCRP.org. Here’s what’s changed on our site — and how we hope it will better serve you. 

Following up on our previous website launch and brand refresh, we’re excited to share the next milestones: a new homepage, upgraded features, and a complete rebuild of the site’s underlying foundation — what we like to call the 'bones' of OCCRP.org. 

You will notice that the homepage is wider, the logo bolder, and that there’s generally more to see on the homepage. We want to make it easier to find what you’re looking for as well as be inspired by everything we have to offer.

We’ve rebuilt the site to be mobile-first, because that’s how most of you read our stories. Our editors can now embed source documents and interactive elements directly into articles, making our work more transparent. We’ve also updated our layouts to better showcase our storytelling in digital and audio formats. 

While the design changes are easy to see, even more has changed under the hood. This new infrastructure makes our site more nimble and ready for continuous updates down the road.

title: A Kidney Transplant, Ignored Advice, and a President’s Surprise Pick to Run a $160 Billion Pacific Island Mine
content:
Almost 40 years after it descended into a devastating civil war, the autonomous region of Bougainville is on the cusp of achieving independence from Papua New Guinea. At its heart sits Panguna, a long-shuttered gold and copper mine worth an estimated $160 billion.

To relaunch the Panguna mine and generate the type of economic development that could support the impoverished region’s bid for full sovereignty, Bougainville’s majority state-owned mining company spent around 10 months on a public search for an international partner, speaking to some of the world’s largest and most experienced mining companies.

But last November, Bougainville President Ishmael Toroama made a shock announcement: he had signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to redevelop the mine with Lloyds Metals and Energy Ltd, a publicly-traded Indian company with no background in major copper and gold extraction.

title: Armenia Detains Ex-President Kocharyan in Corruption Probe
content:
Armenian authorities detained former President Robert Kocharyan and his son Sedrak on Tuesday as part of a corruption investigation into the alleged acquisition of state property at below-market prices. The country’s Anti-Corruption Committee said six people had been detained and alleged that the former president and people close to him used his official position to remove valuable assets from the state, acquire them at significantly reduced prices and subsequently conceal their ownership through affiliated companies. 

Kocharyan’s office called the operation another “attack by the authorities against President Kocharyan and his family.” 

The former president has previously rejected corruption allegations against him as politically motivated. OCCRP reported in 2019 that Kocharyan had been accused of accepting bribes while in office; his lawyer told OCCRP at the time that the allegations were fabricated. A court found there was insufficient evidence to support the corruption allegation at the level of reasonable suspicion.

title: Kazakhstan’s Election Brings a New Parliament — and More Pressure on Journalists
content:
Kazakhstan’s first election to a new unicameral Parliament on Sunday gave a commanding victory to the newly formed, pro-presidential Adilet, or “Justice,” party, in a vote that press-freedom advocates said was held amid mounting pressure on independent journalists.

Adilet won 71.17 percent of the vote, or about 6.5 million ballots, while turnout was 74 percent, according to results released Tuesday by Kazakhstan’s Central Election Commission. Four other parties cleared the five-percent threshold.

None of the seven parties that took part in the election could be seen as opposing President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s policies, according to international observers.

The new 145-seat legislative body is elected entirely through a proportional representation system based on party lists.

The new unicameral Parliament, called the Kurultai, was established earlier this year following constitutional reforms promoted by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. It replaced Kazakhstan’s former two-chamber parliament, abolishing the upper house and the mixed electoral system under which voters could also choose candidates directly, rather than only from party lists.

title: Europol Warns of Violent Shift in European Museum Heists
content:
Europol is warning of an alarming shift in museum heists across Europe, as criminal networks abandon traditional stealth in favor of brute force and extreme violence, according to a report published Monday.

The European Union’s law enforcement agency said perpetrators are increasingly ditching the traditional “deception and discreet execution” of art theft, historically viewed as a “non-violent form of organized property crime,” in favor of direct and confrontational methods.

Instead of niche experts, Europol’s report—”Changing Tactics, Changing Targets: The Evolving Nature of Museum Heists”—found that these new heists are often carried out by decentralized groups of opportunistic criminals recruited via social media on a “crime-as-a-service” basis. These new criminal profiles are increasingly armed with sledgehammers, axes, crowbars, and explosives and firearms to breach premises, smash display cases and intimidate or assault staff in broad daylight.

title: Philippines Arrests South Korean Woman Over Alleged $3.9B Online Gambling Operation
content:
Philippine immigration authorities have arrested a 29-year-old South Korean woman wanted in her home country for allegedly helping operate 23 illegal online gambling websites that generated about 5.33 trillion won ($3.9 billion), the country’s Bureau of Immigration said.

Kim Youngsun was detained on August 7 in General Trias, Cavite, in an operation coordinated with South Korean authorities and the Philippine National Police. The Incheon District Court issued a warrant for her arrest in April 2025, and Interpol published a Red Notice two months later. Authorities allege that Kim worked as an assistant manager and supervised several units of the gambling operation, which was run from offices in Pasay and Quezon City beginning in 2018. She is being held at the Bureau of Immigration’s Warden Facility pending custodial proceedings.

OCCRP asked the Philippine Bureau of Immigration to forward a request for comment to Kim but had not received a response by the time of publication.

title: Moscow Funds Pro-Kremlin Influence Hub in Belarus
content:
A Moscow-funded cultural center in Minsk has operated as an ideological influence hub for the Kremlin, using hundreds of thousands of dollars in Russian state funds to promote the “Russian world” ideology and cement Moscow’s grip over Belarus, according to leaked internal documents.

The cache of more than 270,000 emails from the Moscow House of Compatriots - obtained by Danish public broadcaster DR and analyzed by OCCRP’s Belarusian member center Buro Media - reveals the scale of Russia’s soft-power spending in its neighbor’s capital.

The House of Moscow in Minsk is the Belarusian branch of the Moscow House of Compatriots, a Russian state organization that works with Russian-speaking communities abroad. Although conceived as a business bridge between Moscow and Minsk, it instead hosted events promoting Russian language, joint historical identity, and Kremlin geopolitical priorities.

These efforts mirror Russia’s so-called “humanitarian policy abroad” - a foreign policy doctrine approved by President Vladimir V. Putin that emphasizes defending the ideals of Russkiy Mir, or the “Russian world,” and countering what Moscow labels “Russophobia.”

title: Liberia Charges Ex-Vice President in Transnational Drug Probe
content:
Liberian prosecutors have charged former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor with drug trafficking, money laundering, and other offenses in connection with an investigation into an alleged transnational narcotics network, the country’s authorities announced late Wednesday.

Howard-Taylor, who served as vice president from 2018 to 2024, was arrested on August 19, 2026, at Roberts International Airport and taken to the headquarters of the Liberia National Police, according to a statement from the Ministry of Information.

In a separate Facebook statement, the Information Ministry confirmed that the charges stem from a record $317 million drug bust on July 21, 2026, when officers seized nearly four metric tons of cocaine in Duazon, east of the capital Monrovia. Two foreign nationals were arrested during the operation, which authorities described as the one of the largest narcotics bust in the country's history: one holding dual Spanish and Colombian passports and the other a Serbian passport.

title: Zelenskyy Dismisses Senior Aide Suspected in $3.3 Million Money Laundering Case
content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed senior aide Iryna Mudra on the same day she said anti-corruption investigators had notified her of suspicion in a case involving the alleged laundering of 150 million hryvnias ($3.3 million).

Zelenskyy removed Mudra as deputy head of the Presidential Office without giving a reason for the move.

Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office said in an official ⁠video that their operation, codenamed “Forest Gump,” had uncovered a group that allegedly laundered criminal proceeds through the formal financial system.

According to investigators, the group included a deputy head of the Ukrainian Presidential Office, a former member of parliament, the chair of the management board of a state-owned bank, the chair of its supervisory board and others. The authorities did not identify them by name in the video.

The 150 million hryvnias in cash was allegedly moved through accounts belonging to shell companies and then used to post bail for an alleged member of a criminal organization investigated in the separate “Midas” corruption case. The video did not identify the person whose bail was paid.

title: French Authorities Investigate Widespread Government Data Breaches
content:
French authorities are investigating a series of major cyberattacks after a hack of the Ministry of Public Action and Accounts compromised the personal and financial data of nearly 700,000 individuals and businesses. The stolen records—which include taxable income, family quotient data, withholding tax rates, land registry records, and probate files—came to light after being put up for sale on a hacking forum.

The French National Police’s anticybercrime unit is leading the investigation into the breach. The incident follows a separate late-July cyberattack targeting the Ministry of National Education, with media reports indicating that the same hacker claimed responsibility for selling data extracted from both government systems.

Additionally, ministry officials disclosed that hackers compromised Bloctel, an official government service that allowed users to block telemarketing calls before shutting down on August 11. That breach exposed files containing 3 million phone numbers.

title: Interrogation Tapes Reveal Journalist Murder Suspect Pointing to Highest Levels of Maltese Power
content:
Audio recordings of police interrogations played to a Maltese jury this week revealed that Yorgen Fenech, the businessman on trial for the 2017 car bomb assassination of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, pointed the finger at the highest levels of government at the time, claiming the murder was commissioned by the former prime minister’s chief of staff.

Caruana Galizia, 53, who spent years reporting on corruption at the top of the Maltese state, was killed by a car bomb in October 2017. 

In police interviews recorded in November 2019, he told investigators that Keith Schembri, then chief of staff to Prime Minister Joseph Muscat, had pressed him for years to arrange the murder. Fenech said that the more than 450,000 euros he subsequently paid to the confessed middleman Melvin Theuma was not a murder fee, but money extorted from him through blackmail.

"Everything started with Keith Schembri," Fenech told Superintendent Kurt Zahra during the interrogation. "I was commissioned by Keith Schembri. He was pushing for this murder. I was never the one who sent anyone or did anything."

title: US Charges Eight More Iranians in Global Hacking Case
content:
U.S. prosecutors have charged eight additional Iranians in an alleged state-linked hacking campaign that targeted universities, companies and government agencies worldwide. The expanded indictment brings the number of defendants linked to the Tehran-based Mabna Institute to 17, nine of whom were originally charged in 2018. Prosecutors allege the institute carried out attacks for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and other Iranian clients.

The hackers allegedly targeted more than 100,000 academic accounts and compromised around 8,000 of them at 322 universities, stealing at least 31.5 terabytes of research and intellectual property, the U.S. Justice Department said. They also allegedly breached companies, U.S. government agencies, the United Nations and UNICEF, and sold stolen academic materials through Iranian websites. The U.S. State Department is offering rewards of up to $10 million for information leading to the location of five of the defendants.

title: Indonesia Seizes Record 2.6 Tons of Meth in Major Bust, 10 Arrested
content:
Indonesian authorities have seized 2.6 metric tons of liquid methamphetamine hidden aboard a Tanzanian-flagged vessel in one of the country’s largest drug busts, the National Narcotics Agency announced Tuesday, according to state news agency Antara.

Officers discovered the liquid methamphetamine stored in eight water barrels and inside the water tank of the MV Ocean Porter. Authorities also found a 40-foot container holding 157 boxes of illegal cigarettes on board. Ten crew members, all Myanmar nationals, were arrested.

The operation marks the second major drug intercept involving a Tanzanian-flagged vessel this month, following the confiscation of nearly 1.3 metric tons of ketamine in a separate operation.

title: Iran Moves to Outlaw All Contact With "Hostile" Foreign Media
content:
Iran’s parliament has approved the general framework of a bill that would criminalize speaking to or sharing data with foreign media outlets deemed "hostile." Human rights groups warned that the move is a dangerous attempt to isolate the country from the outside world and hide evidence of internal dissent.

The preliminary vote advances legislation that would prohibit citizens from giving interviews, communicating, or sharing information with external news organizations, particularly those affiliated with the United States or Israel. Under the draft bill, violators face between six months and two years in prison, RFE/RL’s Persian section, Radio Farda, reported. 

Iranian officials framed the proposed law as a vital national security measure. Abbas Goudarzi, a spokesman for the parliamentary presidium, told state media that any communications that “facilitate foreign influence” over Iran would be outlawed under the new statute.

To become law, the bill's specific provisions must be debated by lawmakers and in the end approved by the Guardian Council, a 12-member body of clerics and jurists responsible for vetting all legislation for compliance with Islamic law and the Iranian constitution.

title: A Key Food Source Collapsed Off West Africa’s Coast as Chinese Ships Ground the Species Into Fishmeal
content:
As the day draws to a close in Bubaque, a remote island in Guinea-Bissau, fishermen are arriving with their day’s catch, pulling canoes onto a muddy bank teeming with crabs.

It’s a common scene here in the Bijagós Archipelago, and elsewhere along the West African coast. And one species is especially prized as a source of high-quality protein — the sardinella.

But the small and silvery fish has been decimated in Guinea-Bissau’s coastal waters, according to an internal fisheries assessment produced for the government and obtained by OCCRP.

The assessment was carried out in 2025 by the Atlantic branch of the Russian Federal Research Institute of Fisheries and Oceanography (VNIRO), which worked with scientists from INIPO, Guinea-Bissau’s oceanographic institute. 

While the assessment does not delve into the cause of the decline, a government official attributed it to the recent rise of the local fishmeal industry, which grinds up large volumes of the sardinella and other fish to make a nutrient-dense powder that is fed to farm animals around the world.
snippet: As the day draws to a close in Bubaque, a remote island in Guinea-Bissau, fishermen are arriving with their day’s catch, pulling canoes onto a muddy bank teeming with crabs.

title: US Unseals 25-Count Indictment in $165M Crypto Case
content:
Federal prosecutors in Georgia have unsealed a 25-count indictment against an American man accused of orchestrating a $165 million cryptocurrency Ponzi scheme that defrauded thousands of investors, just days after authorities in Fiji apprehended him and handed him over to federal agents.

The indictment, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, marks the culmination of an international hunt for Edward Zimbardi, 59, who prosecutors say promised up to 25 percent monthly returns through high-yield investment platforms before fleeing to the South Pacific as federal regulators closed in.

Zimbardi was scheduled to appear in federal court in Los Angeles on Monday on 12 counts of wire fraud, 12 counts of money laundering, and one count of money laundering conspiracy. He did not respond to an earlier request for comment.

“Zimbardi allegedly tricked thousands of people into investing in his ‘Crypto Program’ with false promises of enormous returns. Instead, he spent the money on risky currency trades, payments to early investors, and treating himself to a house and expensive vehicles,” U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg said in a statement.

title: Fiji Hands Over a Man Suspected of Ponzi-style Crypto Investment Schemes to US
content:
Fiji handed over an American citizen suspected of involvement in multi-million-dollar cryptocurrency Ponzi schemes across the United States that promised participants returns as high as 25 percent a month and encouraged them to recruit friends and acquaintances for bonuses.

The suspect, Edward Zimbardi, 59, was “removed” from Fiji and returned to the United States last week as part of a joint operation by the FBI and Fiji’s Ministry of Immigration, senior Fiji immigration officials told OCCRP.

Zimbardi did not respond to a request for comment, and it was not immediately clear if he had been formally charged in the United States. The U.S. embassy referred questions to the FBI and the U.S. Department of Justice, and Fijian immigration officials said an FBI announcement was expected in the coming days.

Zimbardi’s legal troubles began in 1997 when he was convicted in Georgia of felony theft and served roughly 17 months in prison.

title: Iraqi Electricity Official Arrested With Millions in Cash as Anti-Graft Campaign Expands
content:
In what appears to be the latest escalation of a sweeping anti-corruption campaign launched by Iraq’s new prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, federal authorities have arrested the undersecretary of the Ministry of Electricity, seizing millions of dollars in cash and gold bars from his properties.

The official, Khalid Ghazay Atiya, was arrested on Aug. 14 by the Federal Commission of Integrity on charges of corruption and illicit enrichment, according to the country’s official Iraqi News Agency.

Investigators executed search warrants at Atiya's residences, uncovering $5.839 million and 1.175 billion Iraqi dinars (nearly $900,000) in cash, alongside seven gold bars and alloys. The commission submitted the seized assets to an investigating judge for further legal action.

title: Spain Seizes 13 Tonnes of Nitrous Oxide in Tenerife
content:
Spain’s Civil Guard dismantled an alleged criminal organization accused of illegally importing and distributing nitrous oxide, commonly known as laughing gas, in Tenerife, seizing nearly 13 tons of the substance in what authorities called Europe’s second-largest haul.

Six people were arrested and another six placed under investigation for alleged involvement in a criminal organization, drug trafficking, trafficking in substances harmful to health, and money laundering, the Civil Guard said. During searches in Arona, Adeje and Granadilla de Abona, officers seized 10,394 containers holding almost 13,000 kilograms of nitrous oxide, as well as 63,500 euros (US$74,000) and 1,000 pounds (US$1,350) in cash.

Authorities also confiscated cocaine, hashish, marijuana and “tusi,” along with imitation firearms and bladed weapons. Investigators said the alleged organization was headed by members of one family and divided into branches responsible for importing the gas from abroad, storing it in properties around the island, and distributing it to customers. The investigation remains ongoing and further arrests are possible, according to the Civil Guard.

title: Former U.S. Banker Jailed for Laundering Medicare Funds
content:
A former Brooklyn bank manager was sentenced to 18 months in prison for helping an international criminal syndicate launder millions of dollars derived from a sprawling $10.6 billion Medicare fraud scheme, the ⁠U.S. Department of Justice said Wednesday.

Renat Abramov, 37, worked as a relationship manager at a bank branch in Brooklyn’s Sheepshead Bay neighborhood. Prosecutors said he acted as a “concierge banker” for participants in the scheme, opening accounts for people who appeared on paper to own medical equipment companies.

More than $8 million in fraud proceeds passed through the accounts, according to the Justice Department. Abramov also helped the nominal company owners make wire transfers, provided information about the accounts and facilitated the transfer of funds offshore.

Abramov ⁠pleaded guilty in February to conspiracy to commit money laundering. His conviction marked the first time the Justice Department’s Health Care Fraud Unit had convicted a former bank employee of conspiring to launder health care fraud proceeds.

title: FAQ: What to Know About Ireland’s Probe Into Our Reporting on Its Alumina Exports to Russia
content:
After OCCRP and partners published an investigation in March exposing how Europe’s largest alumina refinery was feeding into a supply chain linked to Russian weapons manufacturers, the reaction was big. 

Lawmakers and officials across Europe called for Brussels to halt all exports of alumina — the key input needed to produce aluminum — to Russia, in hopes of dealing another blow to Putin’s war machine. 

In Ireland, where the factory is based, the government promised to investigate the matter, and announced late last month that it had shared the findings of its probe with the European Commission. 

The report has not been made public, but The Irish Times obtained a leaked copy and shared it with OCCRP and other media partners. 

Here is what the leaked report says, what remains unknown, and what could come next. 

As a key resource for industries ranging from energy to defense, the powdery precursor to aluminum known as alumina has been branded a “critical raw material” by the European Union, whose leaders have called on member states to stockpile the good as a bulwark against hostile powers.

title: Tapes Hidden in an Ice Cream Box Lay Bare a Maltese Journalist’s Assassination
content:
Secret audio recordings captured on a device hidden in a sock, along with text messages presented in a Maltese courtroom, laid bare the mechanics behind the 2017 assassination of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia—linking a prominent tycoon to hitmen, cash payoffs, and high-level government leaks.

The recordings were played at the trial of Yorgen Fenech, the businessman accused of ordering the assassination. Caruana Galizia, 53, was killed by a car bomb placed beneath the driver’s seat of her vehicle and detonated remotely via SMS on the outskirts of Mosta.

Five men—George Degiorgio, Alfred Degiorgio, Vince Muscat, Robert Agius, and Jamie Vella—have all been convicted for their roles in the murder. Fenech denies any involvement and has pleaded not guilty.

The tapes were recorded by Melvin Theuma, a confessed middleman who was granted a presidential pardon in exchange for evidence. Theuma hid the recorder in his sock and began taping Fenech in April 2018, months after the hitmen were arrested.

“I started recording Yorgen because I needed the proof,” he told jurors. “I knew they were going to betray me either by killing me or throwing me in jail.”

title: Dutch Court Hears Case against Whistleblower’s Murder Suspect
content:
Just five days before a whistleblower who exposed a sprawling illegal gambling network was gunned down in the Netherlands, police briefly detained a key suspect in the killing after intercepting him in a car packed with weapons and bearing stolen licence plates, a Dutch court heard on Wednesday.

Cemil Önal had warned authorities for weeks that his life was in danger after he leaked details of what he claimed was a multi-million-dollar bribery ring linking organized crime to Turkish public officials.

Nevertheless, the former finance director for Turkish Cypriot casino kingpin Halil Falyalı, was gunned down on a hotel terrace in the town of Rijswijk, Netherlands in May 2025. 

The suspect, Hasan Y., a 31-year-old Turkish national, was stopped by police on April 25 in the town of Barneveld in a vehicle with stolen plates. Officers impounded the car but released Hasan Y. It was only after his release that investigators searched the vehicle thoroughly and discovered a Glock pistol and ammunition inside.

By the time police realized what was in the car, it was too late. On a hotel terrace in the Dutch town of Rijswijk, Önal was shot dead.

title: Treasury Rolls Back Ownership Reporting Obligations for U.S. Companies
content:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury has permanently eliminated beneficial ownership reporting requirements for domestic companies and individuals under the Corporate Transparency Act, gutting a major federal anti-money-laundering disclosure program for American small businesses.

The rule effectively exempts U.S. citizens operating domestic businesses from disclosing their beneficial ownership information as was mandated under the Corporate Transparency Act, a landmark anti-corruption law enacted in December 2020, aimed at combating money laundering and illicit finance.

Under the update, foreign companies must still report beneficial ownership information for foreign individuals to FinCEN. However, foreign companies are exempt from reporting ownership information regarding U.S. citizens, as well as details about Americans who assist them in registering to conduct business within the U.S.

FinCEN also announced that it will delete all previously collected information regarding U.S. business owners from its beneficial ownership database.

title: Iraq PM’s Anti-Corruption Campaign Rumbles On
content:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi signaled this week that all corrupt officials — no matter how powerful — would face justice, as his high profile anti-graft campaign saw arrest warrants issued for a particularly prominent former government minister. 

“There are no red lines in pursuing the corrupt... and we call on the ladies and gentlemen of parliament to exercise their oversight role in supporting the government's efforts to combat corruption and dry up its sources,” al-Zaidi posted on his Facebook page Tuesday. 

The premier made the comment after the state Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported on Sunday the Baghdad/Karkh Court of Appeal had issued two arrest and search warrants for former Minister of Labor and Social Affairs, Ahmed Jasim Saber al-Asadi.

Al-Asadi is a former spokesperson for a group of Iran-backed militias central to Iraq’s security apparatus and a leader in the Shiite political alliance that was key to forming the premier’s government. The charges against Al-Asadi allege unexplained enrichment and “awarding contracts in violation of the law to benefit himself and others,” the INA reported.

title: Lebanon Issues New Charges Against Former Central Bank Chief Riad Salame
content:
A Lebanese judge has issued new charges against former central bank governor Riad Salame and a former commercial banker over allegations of financial crimes, including embezzlement, money laundering, bribery, and illicit enrichment, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.

On Monday, Judge Raja Hamouche filed proceedings against 76-year-old Salame and Samir Hanna, 88, the former head of Bank Audi, one of Lebanon's largest banks. The allegations include the creation of shell companies, misappropriating funds belonging to the Central Bank, and the fraudulent use of those funds to purchase shares and bonds in commercial banks. He also charged them with illicit enrichment, money laundering, and bribery.

The Public Prosecutor of Appeal requested an arrest warrant against Salame. Media have reported that he is currently under medical supervision at a hospital in Beirut. He has repeatedly denied all charges against him. His lawyer has not responded to OCCRP’s request for comment.

Hanna, 88, has reportedly already paid a $1 million bail and is not in custody. He could not be reached for comment.

title: French Prosecution Says Alleged 'DZ Mafia' Gang Leader Arrested in Algeria
content:
Algerian authorities have arrested an alleged leader of the ‘DZ Mafia,’ an organized crime syndicate linked to a wave of drug violence in France. Mehdi Laribi, a French-Algerian national, was arrested in Algeria in late July under an arrest warrant issued by investigating magistrates from the Marseille Public Prosecutor's Office. 

The Marseille Public Prosecutor's Office confirmed to OCCRP that Laribi “was detained by Algerian authorities on July 20” and placed under judicial supervision by the Algerian justice system the following day. 

“This action was taken pursuant to an arrest warrant issued by investigating magistrates in connection with the "Octopus” operation handled by the Marseille courts—which concerns the structure of the ‘DZ Mafia’.”

French prosecutors accuse the DZ Mafia of operating a widespread criminal network involved in drug trafficking, kidnapping, and contract killings. Named after Algeria's alpha-2 country code (DZ) in reference to its founders' origins, the group originated in Marseille's housing projects before expanding into several other French cities.

title: Albania's Cheerful 'AI Minister' Is the Product of a Government Agency Under Investigation for Massive Corruption
content:
Last September, Albania made headlines around the world when it introduced the world’s first-ever “AI minister.”

Diella, which means “Sun” in Albanian, was a chatbot that had been promoted to ministerial status. Her remit, Prime Minister Edi Rama announced, was to ensure that “public tenders will be 100 percent free of corruption.”

“I do not have personal ambitions or interests,” the AI avatar, who dresses in traditional costume, told parliament in her maiden speech. “I only have data, a thirst for knowledge, and algorithms dedicated to serving citizens… free from prejudice, discrimination, clientelism, nepotism, or corruption.” 

At the time, there were doubts over whether Diella could offer any real solution to Albania’s long-standing corruption problem. 

It appears that some of the reservations may have been well-founded. Experts caution that Albania’s plan to use Diella as a buffer against corruption has flaws, given that information generated by AI is not inherently neutral, and that there has been little transparency so far on how the technology will be deployed.

title: Alleged Irish Crime Boss Charged After UAE Extradition
content:
Alleged Irish crime boss Daniel Kinahan was extradited from the United Arab Emirates to Ireland on Sunday and charged with directing the activities of a criminal organization.

Kinahan, 49, appeared before Dublin’s non-jury Special Criminal Court less than two hours after arriving aboard an Irish government jet, according to coverage by Irish Times security and crime editor Conor Lally. Kinahan was remanded in custody at the maximum-security Portlaoise Prison and is due to appear in court again on October 5.

He faces a single charge of directing a criminal organization between October 18, 2015, and April 6, 2017. Kinahan has not entered a plea, but has previously denied being a crime boss.

The Irish Times reported that Kinahan did not have a lawyer at the hearing. When Judge Patrick McGrath asked about the lack of legal representation, Kinahan said: “I didn’t have time to arrange anything.” He explained that he had been isolated in a Dubai prison before the extradition and had expected a relative to contact a lawyer.

After the judge explained that any application for bail would have to be made to the High Court, Kinahan replied: “I think we know I won’t be getting bail.”
snippet: Alleged Irish crime boss Daniel Kinahan was extradited from the United Arab Emirates to Ireland on Sunday and charged with directing the activities of a criminal organization.

title: Alleged ‘Enforcer’ in Prince Group Scam Network Identified
content:
An individual identified as “Co-Conspirator-2” in a U.S. grand jury indictment allegedly acted as an “enforcer” for the Prince Group by fending off police crackdowns on the  sprawling Cambodian conglomerate accused of running major cyber scams.

The indictment did not disclose the identity of Co-Conspirator-2, but it contained enough personal information for reporters to confirm that the person is Chen Sokly, who was born in China and has lived in the U.S. and Singapore. 

The indictment targets Prince Group Chairman Chen Zhi, who is charged with alleged wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy. Chen Zhi was extradited from Cambodia to China where he also faces charges. The U.S. court documents obtained by OCCRP do not show any plea, and a spokesperson for the District Court for the Eastern District of New York declined to provide an update on the status of the case. 

A spokesperson for the Prince Group rejected the U.S. Justice Department’s allegations, telling OCCRP they would “challenge these accusations [and] expose the factual and chronological impossibilities on which they rest.”

In the indictment, U.S. prosecutors cited seven anonymized co-conspirators.

title: Spanish-Led Operation Busts Violent Mediterranean Smuggling Ring
content:
A Spanish-led international police operation supported by Europol arrested 78 suspects in Spain and Algeria, dismantling an alleged violent smuggling network across the western Mediterranean, Europol stated Friday. Functioning like a maritime logistics company, the syndicate allegedly utilized an illicit fleet of prohibited "ghost speedboats" to traffic migrants, weapons, fugitives and drugs between Europe and Algeria, employing extreme violence and contract killers to maintain control.

During raids across 17 locations in Spain, officers seized 18 high-speed vessels valued at more than 5 million euros ($5.78 million), alongside firearms, cash, and significant quantities of MDMA, hashish and cocaine. The network allegedly generated an estimated 24 million euros ($27.77 million) from migrant smuggling alone, charging up to 12,000 euros ($13,886) per person for life-threatening sea crossings. The network also allegedly acted as a service provider for other organized crime groups and laundering profits through an informal "hawala" financial system.

title: US Charges NFT Founder in Alleged $10M Investor Fraud
content:
A U.S. federal grand jury has indicted the founder and sole owner of crypto startup Few and Far, on securities and wire fraud charges over an alleged scheme to divert millions of dollars raised from investors to online gambling and personal expenses.

Taj Tarsha, 34, of Miami, was arrested June 6, and his case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge Lewis A. Kaplan, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York said. Each count carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if he is convicted.

Few and Far told investors it was developing a decentralized marketplace for non-fungible tokens, or NFTs. Beginning in February 2022, prosecutors say, Tarsha solicited investments through Simple Agreements for Future Tokens, under which investors paid upfront for the right to receive the startup’s FAR tokens at a later date. Offering documents said the money would be used to develop both the marketplace and the token.

title: Spain and Ecuador Bust International Drug Ring, Seize 21 Tonnes of Cocaine
content:
Police in Spain and Ecuador arrested 44 suspects and seized 21 tonnes of cocaine in a multi-year operation targeting an international drug ring allegedly financed by Dubai-based Albanian investors, Spain’s Interior Ministry announced. Investigators revealed that the financiers funneled large sums of money into Spanish companies to camouflage the drug shipments.

The probe began in 2024 after authorities intercepted multiple shipping containers loaded with cocaine in Brazil, Ecuador and the Spanish ports of Málaga, Algeciras and Valencia. The crackdown escalated in March 2025 when Ecuadorian police raided about 50 properties and detained 36 suspects, while Spanish authorities arrested eight others across several provinces and seized 1 million euros ($1.15 million) in cash.

title: From Headlines to Impact: Connecting Journalism and Civil Society to Drive Accountability in Ukraine
content:
Navigating the intersecting frontlines of a brutal war and structural state reforms, OCCRP and a network of Ukrainian partners have introduced a new approach for driving reform and accountability in the country. 

Established in 2025, this collaborative framework aims to advance deep-dive investigative journalism and connect those findings to the policy efforts of leading advocacy groups. By linking high-impact reporting with civil society expertise, the partners work to expose wrongdoing, trigger concrete legal action, close regulatory loopholes, and tighten international sanctions.

While OCCRP’s editorial teams support the work of Ukrainian media partners, the Impact Department coordinates with a network of civil society organizations and the accountability ecosystem. This approach maximizes their complementary strengths while strictly preserving their independence. It draws inspiration from the decade-old Global Anti-Corruption Consortium — a partnership between OCCRP and Transparency International that an external evaluation found to be five times more effective than traditional reporting alone.

title: ‘I terminated this channel’: Inside the Fake Copyright Racket Silencing News Outlets
content:
Independent media often face off against autocratic governments in countries like Georgia. But last week, OCCRP member center Monitori was forced to contact a tech giant to fend off a censorship attempt: YouTube.

When Monitori’s YouTube channel suddenly disappeared, the outlet received an emailed explanation. It had been taken down due to claims of copyright infringement against three videos.

One video featured a collection of luxury Hermès handbags belonging to the wife of a politician. Another video focused on sanctioned judges, while the third detailed cigarette excise tax changes that benefited a government-linked businessman.

Claiming copyright infringement is an increasingly common tactic to silence journalists and civil society, according to Alberto Fittarelli, a senior researcher specializing in disinformation at Toronto-based Citizen Lab. It’s especially hard to fight since the burden of proof is on the victims to challenge accusations of copyright infringement.

title: Six Years On, Victims of Beirut Port Blast Still Waiting For Justice
content:
Six years after a chemical explosion ripped through Beirut’s port, killing more than 200 people and injuring thousands, Lebanon has yet to issue an indictment naming the individuals allegedly responsible for the catastrophic event.

Lebanese Minister of Justice Adel Nassar told OCCRP that he expects the public prosecution will finalize a legal opinion within 60 to 90 days, after which an investigating judge can issue a formal indictment.

“When I asked the public prosecution, they told me that they estimate a timeframe of 60 to 90 days to deliver their requisitions,” Nassar said, adding that he has no knowledge of the document's contents, and that the judiciary acts independently of his office. 

The country's president Joseph Aoun, who took office in early 2025, renewed calls on Monday for the judiciary to hand down an indictment without delay, declaring that “justice, truth, and accountability remain obligations that cannot be erased by time.”

Lebanon’s previous government was heavily criticized for its handling of the investigation, with judges facing relentless obstruction in the form of political pressure and legal challenges.

title: Indian Police Arrest Seven in Cyber Fraud Sweep
content:
Police in the Indian state of Goa arrested seven people and summoned 24 others for questioning in connection with 40 cyber fraud cases that caused nearly $262,000 in losses. About 40 police teams raided more than 40 locations across 11 states, targeting suspects allegedly involved in investment, parcel, sextortion, “digital arrest” and fake hotel-booking scams.

The operation involved cybercrime and regional police units from across Goa, as well as the state crime branch. Officers seized 21 electronic devices for forensic examination and identified 313 suspected mule bank accounts used to receive or transfer fraud proceeds. Investigators are checking the account holders’ backgrounds and possible links to larger organized cybercrime networks, and have contacted police in the states where the accounts were registered.

title: US Fines UBS Record $125M for 'Willful' Anti-Money Laundering Violations
content:
The U.S. Treasury’s financial watchdog fined a record $125 million penalty Monday against UBS Financial Services Inc. for "willful" anti-money laundering violations, including failing to monitor over $10 billion in foreign currency wires and ignoring red flags on high-risk clients. The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network said in a statement that UBS failed to conduct proper due diligence on customers tied to Russia and Latin America, missing warning signs of corruption and money laundering even when an internal affiliate raised concerns.

The penalty is the largest ever imposed on a U.S. broker-dealer and marks FinCEN’s second enforcement action against the firm since 2018 for similar monitoring weaknesses. As part of the latest resolution, UBS admitted to the violations and agreed to hire an independent reviewer to evaluate its compliance program, with a specific focus on illicit finance risks involving cartels, Russia, Iran, and Venezuela.

title: AI Fuels 55% of African Cybercrimes as Losses Top $480 Million, INTERPOL Warns
content:
Artificial intelligence has become a core driver of cybercrime in Africa, contributing to 55 percent of reported incidents across the continent, INTERPOL said Monday in a report.

The international police agency warned that the recorded frequency of AI deployment in criminal activity “represents a dramatic increase from previous years and reflects a fundamental shift in criminal methodology.” Since 2024, cybercrime-related losses have more than doubled from $192 million to $484 million, driven primarily by AI-facilitated scams, credential harvesting, and automated social engineering campaigns.

“Cybercrime has emerged as one of the most significant criminal threats to the region. AI is automating every stage of a cyberattack from reconnaissance and phishing to extortion and evasion,” said Neal Jetton, director of INTERPOL’s cybercrime unit. “AI is automating every stage of a cyberattack from reconnaissance and phishing to extortion and evasion.”

title: Six Indicted in Czech $20M VAT Fraud Case
content:
European prosecutors have indicted five people and a company for allegedly evading more than $20 million in VAT on goods imported from China, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office announced Monday. After clearing the goods through customs in Czechia, the defendants allegedly claimed they had been supplied to companies elsewhere in the European Union. Investigators believe the purported buyers were fictitious and the shipments were instead sent to e-commerce logistics centers and sold to consumers across the bloc.

Four defendants and the company are accused of operating as an organized criminal group, while a fifth defendant allegedly acted independently. If convicted, the four alleged group members face prison terms of up to 13 years and four months, while the fifth defendant faces up to eight years.

title: The Rise and Fall of Kyrgyzstan’s Seemingly Untouchable Security Chief
content:
In a room decorated with colorful balloons and wall murals, a group of Kyrgyz children pose for the camera.

The boys, seated in front, wear traditional kalpak hats and clutch boxed building sets. Behind them, girls wearing yellow dresses and matching bows hold oversized plush dolls.

The children, celebrating the opening of their new kindergarten, are joined by an unusual guest: Standing behind them is a stern-looking man wearing a dark-blue suit and an inscrutable expression. This is Kamchybek Tashiev, at the time the head of Kyrgyzstan’s feared GKNB security service.

Under his leadership, the agency — the Kyrgyz successor to the Soviet KGB — had grown vastly in influence, becoming the country’s most privileged and influential state body. The new kindergarten, opened in 2024 for staff members’ children, was part of a wave of GKNB construction projects that now dot every region.

And the construction spree was only the most visible sign of the agency’s rise. New laws expanded the GKNB’s powers, giving it control over military units, strategic infrastructure, border protection, and even citizenship, while allowing broader use of force, weapons, and the use of false identities.

title: In Malta Courtroom, Murdered Journalist's Son Describes Last Day With His Mother
content:
Matthew Caruana Galizia was at home in Malta working at his laptop on the morning of October 16, 2017, when he heard the explosion that killed his mother, investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

Testifying today before a jury in the trial of businessman Yorgen Fenech, who is charged with commissioning the murder, her son described the last hours he spent with her — and the investigations she was pursuing when she died.

Fenech has pleaded not guilty to charges of complicity and criminal association in the case, which is unfolding in a courtroom in Malta’s capital, Valletta. 

Daphne Caruana Galizia had spent years reporting on government corruption. She was 53 years old when she was killed by a bomb placed under her car seat and detonated remotely by SMS.  

"My mother made me some lunch. She saw I hadn't eaten anything. She had a phone call and left the house,” Matthew Caruana Galizia testified. 

“She came back in. She had forgotten my dad's chequebook — her account was frozen at the time, and he would sign cheques she could use,” he recalled. “Then she left for the last time."

title: Slim Shady: Smugglers Eye Big Profits Running Weight Loss Drugs into Brazil
content:
It’s barely 4 a.m. on a June morning, and already the streets of Ciudad del Este in Paraguay are filling up with traders hustling to buy and sell everything from socks to home appliances.

The city — which sits at the point where Paraguay, Brazil, and Argentina meet — welcomes more than 100,000 people daily across the Puente de Amistad (Friendship Bridge) from Brazil. 

But the frontier is also a hot spot for drug smuggling, human trafficking, and money laundering. 

And now, the city’s smugglers have found a new cash cow in tirzepatide — the generic name for the active ingredient in the popular weight loss drug Mounjaro. 

In recent months “tirze” — originally developed to treat type 2 diabetes — has become a prized product for criminal groups operating on the border, according to official seizure data, smugglers, pharmaceutical industry officials, and social media records.

Seizures of the drug have skyrocketed. So far in 2026, Brazilian customs reported that it has already confiscated more than ten times the amount of vials seized in 2025. Last year, Brazilian bank Itaú BBA estimated the black market revenue of the tirze trade to be $485 million.
